Introduction - June 2011 











#### **Introduction** 

- **T** **_he precious metals have bounced

since the May sell-off, with the platinum group metals improving as markets emerged from their post-earthquake fears.  Silver is bruised and likely to take its cues from gold for now, rather than being the leader when it comes to changes in direction._** 

- **S** **_ome mid-year weakness may be expected. Gold, at over $1,500, is already discounting a panoply of elements of “bad news”.  Investors, both professional and “grass roots”, are largely bullish for the medium-term and with the United States’ conflict  over monetary strategy, plus tensions rising in Europe over fiscal governance, the groundwork has been laid for a test of $1,600 in the fourth quarter, and more high prices into 2012._** 

- **P** **_alladium fundamentals remain robust.  The market needs a little more time to consolidate, but increasing confidence over the recovery in the auto industry (and the unleashing of pent-up demand later this year) should see palladium exceed $900 in the fourth quarter._** 

##### **Monetary Policy still uncertain in the United States while the European system is drawing some internal fire** 

Questions are still unresolved over the United States’ monetary policy once the current “QE2” strategy draws to a close this month.  The fractures within the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) are becoming more apparent, while the warning by ratings agency Moody’s in early June that the United States’ credit rating is under threat has caused temperatures in the political arena to rise further. Meanwhile European Central Bank (ECB) President Trichet has called not only for stronger intervention in the Eurozone 

- **T** **_he exuberance of silver investors has taken a hard knock in recent weeks and, although silver is likely to move higher with gold later this year, silver’s recent action was a sharp reminder of the vicissitudes of exposure to this volatile metal.  We expect silver to struggle to clear $40 in the coming weeks and perhaps test support at $30._** 

- **P** **_latinum, at over $1,800 in early June, may slip towards $1,750 in mid-year in line with the rest of the sector, and as sentiment reacts to a slowing rate of growth in China.  The market remains in surplus, but we expect it to rally through $1,900 towards year end as gold strengthens and the dollar again comes under pressure._**

Trichet calls for stricter governance** Against the continuing undertones of financial instability the European Parliament’s Committee for Economic and Monetary Affairs has agreed to allow central counterparties to accept gold as collateral. This now has to go forward to the plenary vote of the Parliament in July, and if voted through, should classify gold as a highly liquid asset under the next EU Capital Requirement Directive (CRD), the legislation for which is due to be tabled in mid-2011. The first CRD was implemented in 2007 and brought in a supervisory framework within the EU, designed to ensure financial soundness of credit institutions and some investment firms. Discussion with respect to CRD4 have included possible measures to strengthen bank capital requirements for counterparty risk and it is likely that this is the area that would cover the use of gold, if approved. Activity in the exchange traded funds can generally be taken as a proxy for overall professional investment activity and it was clearly the problems with Greek debt that prompted the fresh wave of buying. ##### **Investor activity prompts a rally, but does not follow through** The major exchange traded funds had been light buyers of gold at the end of April, but as the early May price fall gathered momentum some redemptions developed and the selling continued through to mid-month. The reminder of the fragility of the global financial system was enough to generate considerable fresh buying in the middle of the month, when the Standard & Poor’s ratings agency downgraded Greece’s sovereign debt (the impact of the further downgrading, in early June, was more muted).
